Involution of nodules usually starts after 2 weeks, but larger nodules, particularly on the legs, break down to form itchy, painful ulcers up to 2 cm in diameter. Gradual healing occurs over 2 months to leave circular cicatrized scars. Differential diagnosis includes insect bites in the early stages, monkeypox, where the evolution of a large number of lesions is usually rapid, and tropical ulcers which are usually larger with foul, green slough and are slow to heal. Early tanapox and smallpox could be confused, so it is important to make the correct diagnosis. Crusted lesions could be mistaken for anthrax, but the evolution in tanapox is much slower.

Changes occur in all three regions, with the first notable events taking place at the proximal and distal ends. Elongated core cells in the neck of the follicle continue into the epidermis, where they form a strand of cells that lies between the basal and intermediate cell layers. This is the hair tract that marks the position and pathway of the presumptive hair canal. The distal end of the hair peg flattens, and the epithelial cells along this basal border elongate to form a distinct layer that establishes the matrix. The flattened end of the follicle begins to invaginate into the cord, shaping the bulb with the matrix as the roof of the bulb. Mitotic figures are evident in matrix cells, and longitudinally orientated cells, presumably the progeny of the dividing matrix cells, move out of the matrix into the center of the cord, thereby establishing the first layers of the inner root sheath and the hair (the hair cone). Cells of the outer layer of the follicle located adjacent and lateral to the matrix appear to become more loosely associated with one another, perhaps permitting the inward migration of the cells derived from the matrix. Melanocytes aggregate in the matrix and produce melanin ahead of melanocytes in the general body skin, thus making the bulbs of developing hair follicles ideal sites to examine when evaluating skin biopsy samples from a fetus at risk of tyrosinase-negative oculocutaneous albinism. Such samples can be induced to synthesize melanin by the DOPA reaction if the fetus is normal. The fate of the original K1/K10-positive core cells after the matrix begins to function is not clear, but it is possible that they remain as the layer of cells that lies interior from and perpendicular to the columnar cells of the outer layer of the outer root sheath. caption: Clinical features: Meningococcal meningitis is the most common form of the disease, is indistinguishable from other forms of childhood bacterial meningitis, usually responds rapidly to antibiotics, and is associated with little long-term morbidity. Meningococcal septicaemia with shock is more devastating, commonly presenting with nonspecific symptoms of fever, vomiting, headache, abdominal pain, and muscle aches. The rash of meningococcal septicaemia may be very subtle in the early stages and its recognition is imperative if this life-threatening condition is to be diagnosed early and treated effectively. In the early stages of meningococcal infection, the rash may resemble a viral exanthem such as rubella. This erythematous maculopapular rash is non-purpuric, non-pruritic, and often very transient. Following a diligent search of all areas of the body, the purpuric lesions of meningococcal septicaemia are seen in 80–90% of patients. The rash usually occurs within 12–36 hours of the onset of the disease and is characteristically petechial but may blanch early in the course of the infection. In the classic presentation of meningococcal septicaemia, the petechiae are irregular, small, and often have raised centers. Lesions commonly occur on the limbs and trunk but may be found on the head, palms, soles, and mucous membranes. They may also occur on areas subjected to friction or under pressure by clothing. Progression of the rash of meningococcal septicaemia has been shown to relate to the severity of the coagulopathy and prognosis. As the disease becomes more fulminant, lesions coalesce to form large ecchymoses and become hemorrhagic and bullous. These areas of extensive skin involvement may progress to gangrene of the digits or whole limbs. In such severe purpura fulminans, the gangrenous regions are gunmetal grey or blue-black and are well demarcated.

Nail changes are found in 5% to 10% of patients, with higher proportionality in children. Lichen planus often affects only the nail apparatus in children, presenting as longitudinal ridging, splitting, onycholysis, and redness of the lunula. The entire nail matrix may be involved, leading to obliteration of the nail plate due to idiopathic atrophy. Lichen planus can mimic Yellow Nail Syndrome and is characterized by pterygium formation, with fibrotic replacement of the nail matrix and fusion of the proximal nail fold with the nailbed. Additionally, lichen planus is linked to twenty-nail dystrophy of childhood, usually resolving spontaneously. The mucous membranes, particularly the oral mucosa, are also commonly affected, with 15% of patients with oral lichen planus also exhibiting skin lesions. Women comprise 75% of oral lichen planus cases, typically beginning 10 years later than in men. Oral lesions can be reticulate, erythematous, or ulcerative, often presenting multiple patterns with one predominating; the ulcerative form is the most common. Symptoms are least commonly associated with reticulate lesions.

Experts consensus indicates that oral isotretinoin treatment is warranted for severe acne, poorly responsive acne that improves by less than 50% after 6 months of therapy with combined oral and topical antibiotics, acne that relapses off oral treatment, scars, or acne that induces psychological distress. Additionally, agreed indications include gram-negative folliculitis, inflammatory rosacea, pyoderma faciale, acne fulminans, and hidradenitis suppurativa. For severe trunkal acne in patients who tolerate higher doses, treatment may be given in doses up to 2 mg/kg/day. In practice, most patients start at a 20- to 40-mg dose to avoid an early flare, and then increase to 40 to 80 mg/day to limit side effects.

caption: Tinea barbae, also known as ringworm of the beard, tinea sycosis, and barber's itch, is not a common disease. It primarily affects those in agricultural pursuits, particularly those in contact with farm animals. The condition usually presents unilaterally on the neck or face. There are two clinical types identified: deep, nodular, suppurative lesions; and superficial, crusted, partially bald patches with folliculitis. The deep type develops slowly and produces nodular thickenings and kerion-like swellings, typically caused by T. mentagrophytes or T. verrucosum. The swellings are confluent, forming diffuse boggy infiltrations with abscesses. The overlying skin is inflamed, the hairs are loose or absent, and pus may be expressed through the remaining follicular openings. Generally, the lesions are confined to one part of the face or neck in men. The superficial type is characterized by a less inflammatory pustular folliculitis, possibly associated with T. violaceum or T. rubrum. The affected hairs can sometimes be easily extracted. Rarely, E. floccosum may cause widespread verrucous lesions known as verrucous epidermophytosis.

caption: Nummular Eczema (Nummular Neurodermatitis) usually begins on the lower legs, dorsa of the hands, or extensor surfaces of the arms. The primary lesions are discrete, coin-shaped, erythematous, edematous, vesicular, and crusted patches. Most lesions are 20 to 40 mm in diameter. Lesions may form after trauma (Koebner’s phenomenon). As new lesions appear, old lesions expand by tiny papulovesicular satellite lesions appearing at the periphery and fusing with the main plaque. In severe cases, the condition may spread into palm-sized or larger patches. Pruritus is usually severe and possesses the paroxysmal, compulsive quality, and nocturnal timing seen in circumscribed neurodermatitis. Mast cells are noted in close approximation to nerves in lesional skin, and the neuropeptides substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide are increased in lesional skin. Atopic dermatitis frequently has nummular morphology in adolescents, but in atopy the lesions tend to be more chronic and lichenified. Histologically, nummular eczema is characterized by acute or subacute spongiotic dermatitis. Initial treatment consists of simple soaking and greasing with an occlusive ointment, and once to twice a day application.

caption: Paronychia is an inflammatory reaction involving the folds of the skin surrounding the fingernail. It is characterized by acute or chronic purulent, tender, and painful swellings of the tissues around the nail, caused by an abscess in the nail fold. When the infection becomes chronic, horizontal ridges appear at the base of the nail. With recurrent bouts, new ridges appear. The primary predisposing factor that is identifiable is the separation of the eponychium from the nail plate. This separation is usually caused by trauma as a result of moisture-induced maceration of the nail folds from frequent wetting of the hands. This relationship is close enough to justify treating chronic paronychia as work-related in bartenders, food servers, nurses, and others who often wet their hands. The moist grooves of the nail and nail fold become secondarily invaded by pyogenic cocci and yeasts. The causative bacteria are usually S. aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas species, Proteus species, or anaerobes. The pathogenic yeast is most frequently Candida albicans. The bacteria usually cause acute abscess formation or erythema and swelling, and C. albicans most frequently causes a chronic swelling. If an abscess is suspected, applying light pressure with the index finger against the distal volar aspect of the affected digit will better demonstrate the extent of the collected pus by inducing a well-demarcated blanching. Smears of purulent material will help confirm the clinical impression. Myremecial warts may at times mimic paronychia. Subungual black macules followed by edema, pain, and swelling have been reported to be a sign of osteomyelitis caused by S. aureus or Streptococcus viridans in children with atopic dermatitis.
